passage: The group poster for the history project was due Monday, and Anand had drawn most of it. Disha studied the timeline he had drawn and took a breath. Last week she had snapped at him, "You're useless at layouts," and he'd gone silent for two days. Today she said instead, "The dates on the left are hard to read. Could we make them bigger?" Anand's shoulders tightened first, then loosened. "Yeah, I rushed that part," he said. "Show me which ones?" She pointed to three dates. He fixed them in ten minutes and asked, "Anything else unclear?" Disha shook her head. "No, the rest works. I like the colours." They pinned it to the wall.

qa.q: What was due on Monday?
qa.a: The group poster for the history project was due Monday.

qa.q: How did Anand feel at first when Disha pointed out the dates?
qa.a: His shoulders tightened first, which suggests he felt a flash of defensiveness, and then he loosened when he saw she was talking about the dates, not about him.

qa.q: Which of Disha's two comments was more useful, and why?
qa.a: Saying the dates are hard to read gave him a specific thing to fix, while calling him useless gave him nothing to fix and only hurt.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt before giving her feedback this time?
qa.a: Disha was probably careful and a little tense, since she took a breath and remembered how her snap last week had silenced Anand for two days.

grounding: Criticism aimed at the act is usable, and feedback is accepted without collapsing or attacking.

passage: "That paragraph doesn't make sense," Minakshi said, tapping Bhavna's essay. "Which part?" Bhavna asked, gripping her pencil. "The second line. I can't tell who 'they' is." Bhavna groaned. "I'm so bad at this." Minakshi shook her head. "You're not. I'm saying that line is unclear, not that you are. Should I read it aloud so we can hear it?" Bhavna nodded. As Minakshi read, Bhavna said, "Oh, I meant the villagers. I wrote 'they' too early." She fixed it. Then she added, "Can you tell me when something works too? I only hear the bad parts." Minakshi laughed. "The last paragraph made me smile."

qa.q: What did Minakshi say was unclear?
qa.a: Minakshi said the second line was unclear, because it was hard to tell who 'they' is.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna say she was bad at writing?
qa.a: She seemed to feel stung and to take the comment about the line as being about her, which is a common reaction to criticism. Her tight grip on her pencil shows her tension.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that made her feedback easier to use?
qa.a: Minakshi pointed to one line, said the line was unclear and not Bhavna, and offered to read it aloud together.

qa.q: What would you advise Bhavna to do when she hears feedback next time?
qa.a: Ask which part it refers to, as she did, and ask for what works too.

grounding: Constructive criticism targets the plan, and the writer receives it without collapsing.

passage:
In Class 9 our group had one week to make a video on water saving. Hansa was editing. When she showed the first cut, it was a mess: music too loud, the interview cut off halfway.
I said, "Hansa, you're useless at this. Give it to someone else." In front of everyone.
She went very quiet and closed the laptop. For two days she didn't reply in the group.
I felt bad, but I also still thought the video was bad. Both were true. What I hadn't worked out was how to say the second without saying the first.
On the third day I tried again. "The music drowns out the interview, and it stops mid-sentence at 1:20. Can we fix those two bits?"
Hansa opened the laptop. "The music is easy. Show me where at 1:20."
We finished it together that night. It was the best one in class.
- Sahil

qa.q: At what time did the interview stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: It stopped mid-sentence at 1:20.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling after being called useless?
qa.a: Hansa felt hurt and humiliated, closing the laptop and going silent in the group for two days.

qa.q: Which version of Sahil's criticism worked, and why?
qa.a: The second one, which named the loud music and the cut at 1:20, worked because it criticised the video, not Hansa, and gave her something she could fix.

qa.q: How might the rest of the group have felt hearing the first comment?
qa.a: They were probably uncomfortable and maybe wary, since an insult in front of everyone made it riskier to share their own work.

grounding: The account shows a teenager moving from attacking the person to criticising the specific parts of the work.

passage:
Drama club note - Jahnavi (teacher in charge), Friday
Deepak shared his first script for the annual play today. The group had rules: comment on the scene, not the writer.
Riya said the second scene was confusing because we never learn why the brother leaves. Deepak's jaw tightened and he started to say, "Well, maybe you just didn't get it." Then he stopped. He took a breath, wrote something down, and asked, "Which line made it confusing?"
Riya pointed to it. Two others agreed. Deepak nodded and said, "Okay, that part is unclear. I'll add a line where he explains."
Afterwards he told me it was hard. He said the first comment felt like being called a bad writer. I told him that noticing the urge to attack and choosing to ask a question was the most grown-up thing I saw today.
Next week: revised scene two.

qa.q: Which scene did Riya say was confusing?
qa.a: Riya said the second scene was confusing.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when his jaw tightened?
qa.a: He felt defensive and stung, as if the comment called him a bad writer, and nearly snapped back.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that turned the feedback into something useful?
qa.a: He paused, wrote a note, and asked which line was confusing, then agreed the part was unclear and planned a fix.

qa.q: How might Riya have felt when Deepak asked which line instead of snapping?
qa.a: Riya probably felt relieved and respected, and more willing to keep giving honest feedback.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a teenager receiving criticism of his work without attacking and turning it into a usable fix.

passage:
Wednesday
Gopika looked at my science fair poster today and said, "The graph part is unclear. I can't tell which line is which."
My first thought, honestly, was "Well, YOUR poster has spelling mistakes." It was right there in my mouth.
But I didn't say it. I just said, "Hmm," and walked to the water cooler and back. Counted to ten, like Ammi says.
When I came back, I looked at the graph. She was right. Both lines are blue. No labels.
I said, "Okay, which would be clearer, colours or labels?" She said, "Both?" and lent me her red pen.
It's better now. Really better.
The weird thing is, she didn't say my poster was bad. She said one part was unclear. That's why I could fix it and not just feel stupid.
- Hafsa

qa.q: What colour were both lines on the graph?
qa.a: Both lines were blue.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling right after Gopika's comment?
qa.a: Hafsa felt defensive and stung, with an urge to attack Gopika's spelling, before calming down.

qa.q: What small step helped Hafsa accept the feedback?
qa.a: Walking to the water cooler and counting to ten gave Hafsa time to cool down and look at the graph fairly.

qa.q: How does Gopika's way of criticising compare with what Hafsa nearly said?
qa.a: Gopika named one unclear part of the poster, which could be fixed, while Hafsa's retort would have been an attack meant to hurt back.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager accepting criticism of a specific part of the work without attacking, and seeing why that kind is usable.
